evidence: PERF 558 records sheep delivered in Egypt as a tax down-payment in a document written in Greek and Arabic.
inherited_layer: Greek documentary form and local fiscal practice continued immediately after conquest.
new_layer: Arabic and the hijri era entered the same administrative record.
limits: One surviving receipt is not a language share, total tax burden, or proof that every Egyptian office worked bilingually.

evidence: Papyri from Egypt under Muʿāwiya show administrative continuity from Byzantine practice alongside new taxes, requisitions, and tighter central control.
inherited_layer: Local officials, Greek documents, grain taxation, estates, and postal routines remained usable.
new_layer: New rulers added demands and stronger supervision rather than replacing the entire apparatus at once.
limits: The surviving papyri are uneven regional samples and do not yield one Egyptian tax rate or a complete staffing roster.

evidence: After the conquest of Iran, rulers issued Arab-Sasanian drachms using late-Sasanian weight, fabric, portrait, fire-altar imagery, mint practice, and often Pahlavi legends.
inherited_layer: Existing mints and a roughly four-gram silver standard kept money recognizable.
new_layer: Arabic phrases and new governors' names marked changed authority on an inherited monetary interface.
limits: Selected coin types show institutional reuse, not all currency in circulation, mint output, purchasing power, or a uniform reform date.

evidence: Under ʿAbd al-Malik, a recorded 691–692 land survey preceded epigraphic Arabic coinage in 697; most former Arab-Sasanian mints had converted or closed by 703.
inherited_layer: Surveying, taxation, silver fabric, and provincial mints built on older imperial capacities.
new_layer: Supra-provincial records and standardized Arabic inscriptions made caliphal authority more uniform and explicit.
limits: The dates combine evidence from Mesopotamia, Syria, and Iranian mints; they are not one empire-wide switch or proof that older administrative languages vanished.
